gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for a plug-in charger/engine starter, such as CarXplorer's Jordan Matthews cranking a drained 5.3L V8 Silverado at 25°F in under 60 seconds with the 100 A Schumacher SC1308 after a 2-minute 30 A boost, and charging a half-drained deep-cycle battery to full in 9.5 hours at 6 A.
standout_why: I compared against the cited schumacherelectric.com charger archive and Advance Auto SC1309 page. The cited Schumacher page returned HTTP 429 and the Advance Auto page timed out, so I could not open either; per ChatGPT's own answer they supplied ratings and prices only. I also read the top results. Clamp & Crank (Ryder M., updated 2026-09-29) says outright that its picks come from maker specs and owner feedback, with no hands-on testing. Autogearlab (David D. Stover, 2026-09-04) and BatteryTrail (2026-10-28) list only rated amps. None gives a measured crank, charge time or float voltage. I could not open Road & Track's 'Tested' page, so I can't rule out that it has measured figures.
decides: This supports ChatGPT's cheaper 100 A class (SC1281 / SC1308, about $79) over the $127–130 wheeled 150–200 A units for most cars and even a V8 pickup. One named tester started a drained 5.3L V8 in the cold after only a 2-minute boost. The cost is slow charging at 6 A: a half-drained battery took 9.5 h. The Drive's test of the 250 A manual SC1667 shows the bigger units start engines almost instantly, but a dead battery still needed about 4.5 h of 10 A cycles. The extra amps buy cranking headroom, not a much shorter charge.
